screens.title: Collision Detection and Response
screens.narratorSegment: Collision is the invisible grammar that makes a game world feel solid and interactive. In this lesson you will build a practical understanding of collision primitives like capsule, box, and sphere; learn the purpose of collision presets and custom channels; and practise wiring overlap and hit events in C++ so your actors can respond to the world. We focus on predictable behavior: when to use overlap triggers for zones and pickups, when to use hit events for physical impacts, and how project settings and component flags control whether an event fires. You will see a concrete C++ projectile example that binds OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentHit, and you will learn the common mistakes that cause events to silently never fire. By the end you’ll know how to configure a Projectile profile, enable the right flags on components, and debug collision in the editor. Consider a projectile that should trigger a pickup when passing through a trigger volume, yet create a physical impact when striking a wall; knowing the difference between overlap and hit will let you implement both behaviors reliably. Ask yourself: what behavior do I want first — a trigger, or a physical stop? That choice drives the configuration.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice and code changes so you can build reliable collision interactions in UE5. First, you will understand core collision concepts: how collision primitives, presets, channels, object types and responses form the system’s vocabulary. Third, you will implement C++ handlers for overlap and hit delegates so your actor can react to both trigger volumes and physical impacts. Fourth, you will recognize common configuration mistakes and performance costs so you can choose simple shapes and filtering to keep your game responsive. A short mnemonic: Vocabulary, Configure, Code, Diagnose — this sequence keeps you efficient and debuggable when collisions misbehave.

screens.title: Collision Primitives: the geometry of interaction
screens.narratorSegment: Collision primitives are the basic geometric shapes that Unreal Engine uses to detect and respond to intersections. Common primitives include USphereComponent, UBoxComponent, and UCapsuleComponent. These shapes are lightweight and fast compared to complex per-poly meshes, which makes them the preferred choice for runtime collision checks. Practically, you use a capsule for characters because it smoothly slides over obstacles, a sphere for projectiles and radius checks, and a box for simple static triggers. Choose the simplest primitive that models the interaction you need: an over-detailed shape can increase collision checks and degrade performance. A concrete example: a player character uses a UCapsuleComponent for movement collision detection so steps and slopes are handled cleanly; adding per-poly collision to the same actor for cosmetic meshes would be unnecessary and costly. A common misconception is that detailed visual meshes must match collision exactly; instead use simplified collision for physics and reserve per-poly collision only for specific needs. Key takeaway: prefer primitive shapes, match the primitive to the interaction, and reduce per-poly checks to keep the game responsive. How might you simplify a complex object in your level to use a box or capsule instead of per-poly collision?

keyIdea.title: Primitive rule
keyIdea.text: Use sphere, box, or capsule shapes for efficient collision; reserve complex meshes for exceptional cases.

content.html:
Core Concept
Collision Primitives
Simple geometric components that provide the collision geometry used for overlap and hit detection.
USphereComponent
Good for projectiles and radius checks.
UBoxComponent
Works well for triggers and simple world geometry.
UCapsuleComponent
Ideal for character collision and smooth sliding.
Key Takeaway

Prefer simple primitives (sphere, box, capsule) for runtime collision. They are fast, predictable, and easier to debug.

Concrete Example
A projectile uses a USphereComponent with a small radius to detect hits and overlaps reliably. The player's UCapsuleComponent handles movement and prevents clipping on steps.
Common Mistake
Using per-poly collision for every object. This increases queries and can harm frame rate. Simplify collision where you do not need exact visual fidelity.
Check Your Understanding
  • When would a capsule be a better choice than a box?
  • Which primitive is usually best for projectiles and why?

screens.title: Collision Presets and Object Types
screens.narratorSegment: Collision Presets are saved collections of collision responses that you can assign to a component to set its default behavior. Common presets include BlockAll, OverlapAll, PhysicsActor, and NoCollision. They provide fast setup when default behavior is adequate. Object Type, on the other hand, labels a component as belonging to a category such as WorldStatic, Pawn, or Projectile. The runtime collision system compares Object Types and Responses in a matrix: each Object Type has a response to other channels set to Ignore, Overlap, or Block. Custom Collision Channels let you add new categories in Project Settings for gameplay-specific roles like Pickup or ForceField. Use presets to move quickly, and switch to custom channels when you need precise filtering. For example, create a Projectile channel that blocks WorldStatic and Pawn but overlaps Pickup so projectiles can trigger pickable sensors. A frequent misconception is thinking a preset always covers every gameplay need; presets are convenience tools, but the channel matrix is how you express nuanced rules. Takeaway: presets accelerate setup, channels give you control and performance by reducing unnecessary checks. Collision Presets and Object Types means presets are shortcuts; channels and object types define the true interaction matrix — use both together for clarity and performance.. In practical terms, quick presets vs. custom object types for fine control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Presets & Object Types
Presets are ready-made response sets; object types categorize components for matrix-based filtering.
Collision Preset
A convenient profile such as BlockAll or OverlapAll used to assign default responses quickly.
Object Type
Labels the component (e.g., Pawn, WorldStatic, Projectile) used by the response matrix to determine interactions.
Key Takeaway

Use presets for quick setup; use custom channels and object types to precisely control which things block, ignore, or overlap one another.

Concrete Scenario
Create a Projectile object type that blocks world geometry and characters but overlaps pickups. Assign the Projectile preset to your projectile's collision component.
Common Mistake
Relying only on presets without checking the matrix. A preset may not set the response you expect to a custom channel, so always inspect the responses after creating channels.
Quick Checklist
  • Confirm Object Type is correct for the component.
  • Check the response to each relevant channel: Block, Overlap, or Ignore.
  • When in doubt, create a custom Projectile channel for clarity.

screens.title: Overlap Events — triggers and zones
screens.narratorSegment: Overlap events fire when collision shapes intersect without physically stopping each other. Use overlap events for trigger volumes, pickups, or enter/exit zones where actors should pass through but still generate gameplay responses. For an overlap to fire you must enable Generate Overlap Events on at least one of the involved components, and set the collision response between their object types to Overlap. A practical example is a healing zone represented by a UBoxComponent set to Overlap for the Pawn object type; when a player's capsule enters that box, OnComponentBeginOverlap triggers healing logic. A common confusion is expecting overlap events when both sides are set to Block; if both components block each other you will get a hit event instead of an overlap. Another mistake is expecting overlaps when Generate Overlap Events is false on both sides — nothing will fire. When implementing overlaps in C++ you bind OnComponentBeginOverlap with AddDynamic to a UFUNCTION; inside the handler you check OtherActor and OtherComp for validity before applying effects. Takeaway: overlaps detect presence without enforcing physics; use them for non-blocking triggers and pickups. Ask yourself: does this interaction need a physical stop, or only a notification when an actor enters a zone?

keyIdea.text: Overlaps notify presence without physical blocking; ensure Generate Overlap Events is enabled and responses are set to Overlap.

content.html:
Definition
Overlap Events
Non-blocking notifications fired when shapes intersect and at least one side generates overlap events.
Requirements
  • At least one component has Generate Overlap Events = true
  • Collision response between object types is set to Overlap
  • Bind OnComponentBeginOverlap to a UFUNCTION with AddDynamic
Key Takeaway

Use overlaps for triggers and pickups. If you want a physical stop, choose hit-based blocking instead.

Concrete Example
A healing zone is a UBoxComponent set to Overlap the Pawn object type, with Generate Overlap Events enabled. OnComponentBeginOverlap grants health when the player's capsule enters.
Common Mistakes
Forgetting Generate Overlap Events or setting the response to Block or Ignore prevents overlap callbacks. Also, if both sides block, you will not get overlap events.
Check
  • Are both components' object types correct?
  • Is the collision response set to Overlap?
  • Is the handler bound with AddDynamic?

screens.title: Hit Events — physical collisions and impacts
screens.narratorSegment: Hit events occur when two collision primitives physically collide and at least one side prevents passage; they are used for impacts, projectiles striking walls, or an object landing. For hit events to fire you typically need components set to block each other and either Simulate Physics enabled on physics actors or Generate Hit Events / Notify Rigid Body Collision enabled on static/kinematic components. For example, a projectile colliding with a wall should have its collision set to Block the WorldStatic object type and SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) so OnComponentHit will execute. A common confusion is expecting hits when components merely overlap—if both objects are configured to overlap, you will never get a hit. Another mistake is enabling only physics simulation but not the notify flags, which can prevent the engine from calling your delegate. When handling OnComponentHit in C++ check the Hit parameter for impact location and NormalImpulse for force-based responses. Takeaway: hits are for physical responses; ensure both collision responses and physics/notify flags are correctly configured so your impact logic can run reliably. Hit Events — physical collisions and impacts means hit events require blocking interactions and either physics simulation or explicit hit notifications to be enabled.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
Hit Events
Events that fire when collisions physically block movement and contact occurs.
Requirements
  • Collision responses set to Block between involved object types
  • Simulate Physics enabled for physics objects or Generate Hit Events / NotifyRigidBodyCollision enabled
  • Bind OnComponentHit using AddDynamic
Key Takeaway

Use hit events for impacts and physical responses and ensure physics or notify flags are set so the delegate is invoked.

Concrete Example
A thrown object with Simulate Physics enabled collides with a wall set to Block. OnComponentHit provides the impact location and NormalImpulse for playing a sound or spawning an effect.
Common Mistakes
Expecting OnComponentHit when both sides are configured to Overlap, or forgetting to enable Notify Rigid Body Collision on non-physics components.
Check
  • Are responses set to Block between these object types?
  • Is Simulate Physics or Notify Rigid Body Collision enabled where required?

screens.title: Binding events in C++: AddDynamic and UFUNCTION
screens.narratorSegment: Binding collision delegates in C++ connects engine events to your actor logic. The pattern starts with declaring UFUNCTION handlers in the header, then binding those handlers to component delegates in the constructor or BeginPlay using AddDynamic. The example in this lesson shows a projectile actor with a USphereComponent named CollisionSphere. In the header we declare void OnOverlapBegin(...) and void OnHit(...) as UFUNCTIONs. In the constructor we enable SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true) and SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) on the collision component, then call CollisionSphere->OnComponentBeginOverlap. AddDynamic(this, &AMyProjectile::OnOverlapBegin) and CollisionSphere->OnComponentHit. AddDynamic(this, &AMyProjectile::OnHit). A key point: the signatures must match the delegate signature exactly and the UFUNCTION should have no parameters omitted. A common bug is binding before a component is created or forgetting to mark the function as UFUNCTION, which prevents AddDynamic from compiling or working as expected. When you bind correctly, events will call your functions at runtime, permitting logic like destroying a projectile on overlap or spawning an effect on hit. Practice by compiling and verifying your UE_LOG statements appear in the Output Log. In practical terms, how to declare, bind, and enable component delegates in an actor class. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Declare UFUNCTION handlers, enable the right component flags, and bind with AddDynamic to receive overlap and hit callbacks.

content.html:
Process Flow
Bind delegates with AddDynamic
Declare handlers, enable component flags, then bind in constructor or BeginPlay.
// In AMyProjectile.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "MyProjectile.generated.h"

class USphereComponent;
class UProjectileMovementComponent;

UCLASS()
class YOURGAME_API AMyProjectile : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AMyProjectile();

protected:
    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Components")
    USphereComponent* CollisionSphere;

    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Components")
    UProjectileMovementComponent* ProjectileMovement;

    UFUNCTION()
    void OnOverlapBegin(UPrimitiveComponent* OverlappedComp, AActor* OtherActor, UPrimitiveComponent* OtherComp, int32 OtherBodyIndex, bool bFromSweep, const FHitResult& SweepResult);

    UFUNCTION()
    void OnHit(UPrimitiveComponent* HitComp, AActor* OtherActor, UPrimitiveComponent* OtherComp, FVector NormalImpulse, const FHitResult& Hit);
};
Constructor Bindings
Enable overlap and hit notifications, then AddDynamic to bind your functions.
AMyProjectile::AMyProjectile()
{
    CollisionSphere = CreateDefaultSubobject<USphereComponent>(TEXT("CollisionSphere"));
    RootComponent = CollisionSphere;

    CollisionSphere->InitSphereRadius(15.0f);
    CollisionSphere->SetCollisionProfileName(TEXT("Projectile"));

    CollisionSphere->SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true);
    CollisionSphere->SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true);

    CollisionSphere->OnComponentBeginOverlap.AddDynamic(this, &AMyProjectile::OnOverlapBegin);
    CollisionSphere->OnComponentHit.AddDynamic(this, &AMyProjectile::OnHit);
}
Key Takeaway

Bindings must match delegate signatures and the component must have the correct flags enabled for events to fire.

screens.title: Implementing OnOverlapBegin and OnHit handlers
screens.narratorSegment: Once delegates are bound, implement the handler functions to perform gameplay effects or diagnostics. For OnOverlapBegin, check that OtherActor is valid, not this, and that OtherComp exists before acting. A common pattern is to print the OtherActor name to the log and optionally Destroy the projectile. For OnHit, inspect the Hit result to get impact. Location and use NormalImpulse if you need physics-driven responses. The example code logs overlap and hit events using UE_LOG so you can verify behavior in the Output Log. Do not assume the OtherActor is always the expected class — use casting or tags to confirm type before applying damage or destroying. Also avoid heavy work inside the handler; if you need complex processing, queue work to a manager or trigger a Blueprint event. Example handler bodies from the chapter show the minimal safety checks and log statements used during testing. Run your actor in the editor, observe log entries when the projectile passes through a trigger versus when it impacts a wall, and use that evidence to adjust your collision responses or flags. Takeaway: handlers are your bridge between physics events and gameplay code — validate actors, log for debugging, and keep handlers focused.

screens.title: Creating a Projectile Collision Profile
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a custom collision profile lets you express consistent behavior for many actors without repeating individual component setup. In Project Settings under Engine → Collision create a new preset named Projectile. Set its Object Type to WorldDynamic and Collision Enabled to Query and Physics so it participates in both queries and physics interactions. Then configure Collision Responses: set Pawn, WorldStatic, and WorldDynamic to Block so the projectile can impact characters and world geometry; set Pickup or OverlapAllDynamic to Overlap so the projectile triggers pickups without blocking them. Ensure Generate Overlap Events is checked on components that should generate overlap callbacks. The value of a profile is that you can assign it to every projectile’s collision component and change behavior globally from one place. A common pitfall is forgetting to check the Generate Overlap Events checkbox in the profile or on individual components, resulting in overlaps not firing even though the responses are correct. After creating the profile, apply it on your USphereComponent via SetCollisionProfileName(TEXT("Projectile")) or in the editor details. Compile and test: spawn the projectile, verify overlaps with pickups and hits with static walls. Takeaway: profiles save time, reduce errors, and make behavior predictable across many actors.

Create Projectile Profile

screens.title: Overlap vs Hit — choosing the right event
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing overlap or hit depends on the gameplay effect you want. Overlap is for detection without physical blocking — think pickups, zones, and triggers where actors should pass through while your code reacts. Hit is for physical interaction: impacts, blocking movement, and physics responses. A concrete decision example: a healing zone should be an overlap so the player can walk through and receive health. A force field that stops the player requires hit-based blocking and a Block response so movement is halted and OnComponentHit can run if notify flags are enabled. Misconfiguration often comes from assuming both will happen automatically; overlaps occur only if Generate Overlap Events is enabled and the response is Overlap, while hits require Block plus either physics simulation or explicit notify flags. Performance is also a factor: overlaps can be cheaper if filtered correctly and shapes are simple, but enabling many overlap queries or complex per-poly collisions will increase C P U cost. When in doubt, sketch the intended behavior as 'notify only' (overlap) or 'stop and respond' (hit) and adjust object types and flags to match that intent. Final question to consider: does your gameplay require a physical response or merely a notification when objects meet?

screens.title: Diagnosing why an event never fires
screens.narratorSegment: When a collision event does not fire the issue is almost always a configuration mismatch. Use a methodical checklist: first, confirm the involved components exist and are registered as collision-enabled components on the actor. Second, inspect both components' Object Type and Collision Responses — are they set to Overlap or Block as you expect? Third, verify component flags: for overlaps ensure SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true) is set on at least one side; for hits ensure Simulate Physics is enabled where appropriate or SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) is active. Fourth, confirm that your handler is declared with UFUNCTION and bound with AddDynamic without binding before the component is created. Fifth, use the editor's Show → Collision visualization to see the actual shapes and queries at runtime. For debugging include UE_LOG in your handlers or temporary print statements in BeginPlay to confirm the actor exists and binding succeeded. A common oversight is checking only one component; remember both sides influence whether an event fires. The final diagnostic step is to change the response temporarily to OverlapAll or BlockAll to see which event appears, then narrow settings back to the intended configuration. Takeaway: use the checklist and visual debug tools to find configuration mismatches quickly.

Common Mistake
Why an event never fires
A step-by-step checklist to locate configuration issues preventing delegates from being called.
  1. Confirm components are created and registered on the actor.
  2. Check Object Type and Collision Responses on both components.
  3. Ensure Generate Overlap Events or Notify Rigid Body Collision is enabled as required.
  4. Verify UFUNCTION signature matches delegate and AddDynamic binding succeeded.
  5. Use Show → Collision in the editor and observe the Output Log for UE_LOG prints.

Temporarily set the responses to OverlapAll or BlockAll to force a visible event, then adjust the matrix to the intended configuration once you confirm which event fires.

Add UE_LOG at the end of your constructor to confirm your AddDynamic lines ran; missing logs indicate binding did not occur.

screens.title: Build and test: MyProjectile and pickup actor

fullNarratorScript:
Collision is the invisible grammar that makes a game world feel solid and interactive. In this lesson you will build a practical understanding of collision primitives like capsule, box, and sphere; learn the purpose of collision presets and custom channels; and practise wiring overlap and hit events in C++ so your actors can respond to the world. We focus on predictable behavior: when to use overlap triggers for zones and pickups, when to use hit events for physical impacts, and how project settings and component flags control whether an event fires. You will see a concrete C++ projectile example that binds OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentHit, and you will learn the common mistakes that cause events to silently never fire. By the end you’ll know how to configure a Projectile profile, enable the right flags on components, and debug collision in the editor. Consider a projectile that should trigger a pickup when passing through a trigger volume, yet create a physical impact when striking a wall; knowing the difference between overlap and hit will let you implement both behaviors reliably. Ask yourself: what behavior do I want first — a trigger, or a physical stop? That choice drives the configuration.

These objectives focus your practice and code changes so you can build reliable collision interactions in UE5. First, you will understand core collision concepts: how collision primitives, presets, channels, object types and responses form the system’s vocabulary. Second, you will configure custom collision channels and object types in Project Settings, giving you fine-grained control over what collides or triggers. Third, you will implement C++ handlers for overlap and hit delegates so your actor can react to both trigger volumes and physical impacts. Fourth, you will recognize common configuration mistakes and performance costs so you can choose simple shapes and filtering to keep your game responsive. Each objective pairs skill with a why: knowing the terms avoids accidental ignores; setting channels prevents unintended blocking; handling delegates lets you drive gameplay effects such as pickups or explosions; and spotting mistakes keeps the runtime fast. A short mnemonic: Vocabulary, Configure, Code, Diagnose — this sequence keeps you efficient and debuggable when collisions misbehave.

This screen extends objectives into concrete editor tasks and debugging habits. You will create or assign a custom Projectile collision profile in Project Settings and ensure it uses Query and Physics where needed. You will set component flags such as SetGenerateOverlapEvents and SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision so events start firing during play. You will compile and run a simple actor that prints log messages from overlap and hit handlers, then use the editor's Show → Collision debug visualization to confirm shapes and responses. Finally, you will practice a diagnostic checklist: verify object types, confirm response matrix, check flags on both components, and inspect the Output Log for your UE_LOG messages. Each step is practical: change a preset, recompile, spawn the actor, and observe whether your projectile passes through a trigger or hits a wall as expected. This sequence turns conceptual knowledge into repeatable debugging routines you can apply to future interaction systems.

Collision primitives are the basic geometric shapes that Unreal Engine uses to detect and respond to intersections. Common primitives include USphereComponent, UBoxComponent, and UCapsuleComponent. These shapes are lightweight and fast compared to complex per-poly meshes, which makes them the preferred choice for runtime collision checks. Practically, you use a capsule for characters because it smoothly slides over obstacles, a sphere for projectiles and radius checks, and a box for simple static triggers. Choose the simplest primitive that models the interaction you need: an over-detailed shape can increase collision checks and degrade performance. A concrete example: a player character uses a UCapsuleComponent for movement collision detection so steps and slopes are handled cleanly; adding per-poly collision to the same actor for cosmetic meshes would be unnecessary and costly. A common misconception is that detailed visual meshes must match collision exactly; instead use simplified collision for physics and reserve per-poly collision only for specific needs. Key takeaway: prefer primitive shapes, match the primitive to the interaction, and reduce per-poly checks to keep the game responsive. How might you simplify a complex object in your level to use a box or capsule instead of per-poly collision?

Collision Presets are saved collections of collision responses that you can assign to a component to set its default behavior. Common presets include BlockAll, OverlapAll, PhysicsActor, and NoCollision. They provide fast setup when default behavior is adequate. Object Type, on the other hand, labels a component as belonging to a category such as WorldStatic, Pawn, or Projectile. The runtime collision system compares Object Types and Responses in a matrix: each Object Type has a response to other channels set to Ignore, Overlap, or Block. Custom Collision Channels let you add new categories in Project Settings for gameplay-specific roles like Pickup or ForceField. Use presets to move quickly, and switch to custom channels when you need precise filtering. For example, create a Projectile channel that blocks WorldStatic and Pawn but overlaps Pickup so projectiles can trigger pickable sensors. A frequent misconception is thinking a preset always covers every gameplay need; presets are convenience tools, but the channel matrix is how you express nuanced rules. Takeaway: presets accelerate setup, channels give you control and performance by reducing unnecessary checks. Collision Presets and Object Types means presets are shortcuts; channels and object types define the true interaction matrix — use both together for clarity and performance.. In practical terms, quick presets vs. custom object types for fine control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Overlap events fire when collision shapes intersect without physically stopping each other. Use overlap events for trigger volumes, pickups, or enter/exit zones where actors should pass through but still generate gameplay responses. For an overlap to fire you must enable Generate Overlap Events on at least one of the involved components, and set the collision response between their object types to Overlap. A practical example is a healing zone represented by a UBoxComponent set to Overlap for the Pawn object type; when a player's capsule enters that box, OnComponentBeginOverlap triggers healing logic. A common confusion is expecting overlap events when both sides are set to Block; if both components block each other you will get a hit event instead of an overlap. Another mistake is expecting overlaps when Generate Overlap Events is false on both sides — nothing will fire. When implementing overlaps in C++ you bind OnComponentBeginOverlap with AddDynamic to a UFUNCTION; inside the handler you check OtherActor and OtherComp for validity before applying effects. Takeaway: overlaps detect presence without enforcing physics; use them for non-blocking triggers and pickups. Ask yourself: does this interaction need a physical stop, or only a notification when an actor enters a zone?

Hit events occur when two collision primitives physically collide and at least one side prevents passage; they are used for impacts, projectiles striking walls, or an object landing. For example, a projectile colliding with a wall should have its collision set to Block the WorldStatic object type and SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) so OnComponentHit will execute. A common confusion is expecting hits when components merely overlap—if both objects are configured to overlap, you will never get a hit. Another mistake is enabling only physics simulation but not the notify flags, which can prevent the engine from calling your delegate. When handling OnComponentHit in C++ check the Hit parameter for impact location and NormalImpulse for force-based responses. The example in this lesson shows a projectile actor with a USphereComponent named CollisionSphere. In the header we declare void OnOverlapBegin(...) and void OnHit(...) as UFUNCTIONs. In the constructor we enable SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true) and SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) on the collision component, then call CollisionSphere->OnComponentBeginOverlap. A force field that stops the player requires hit-based blocking and a Block response so movement is halted and OnComponentHit can run if notify flags are enabled. Misconfiguration often comes from assuming both will happen automatically; overlaps occur only if Generate Overlap Events is enabled and the response is Overlap, while hits require Block plus either physics simulation or explicit notify flags. Performance is also a factor: overlaps can be cheaper if filtered correctly and shapes are simple, but enabling many overlap queries or complex per-poly collisions will increase C P U cost. When in doubt, sketch the intended behavior as 'notify only' (overlap) or 'stop and respond' (hit) and adjust object types and flags to match that intent. Final question to consider: does your gameplay require a physical response or merely a notification when objects meet?

When a collision event does not fire the issue is almost always a configuration mismatch. Use a methodical checklist: first, confirm the involved components exist and are registered as collision-enabled components on the actor. Second, inspect both components' Object Type and Collision Responses — are they set to Overlap or Block as you expect? Third, verify component flags: for overlaps ensure SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true) is set on at least one side; for hits ensure Simulate Physics is enabled where appropriate or SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true) is active. Fourth, confirm that your handler is declared with UFUNCTION and bound with AddDynamic without binding before the component is created. Fifth, use the editor's Show → Collision visualization to see the actual shapes and queries at runtime. For debugging include UE_LOG in your handlers or temporary print statements in BeginPlay to confirm the actor exists and binding succeeded. A common oversight is checking only one component; remember both sides influence whether an event fires. The final diagnostic step is to change the response temporarily to OverlapAll or BlockAll to see which event appears, then narrow settings back to the intended configuration. Takeaway: use the checklist and visual debug tools to find configuration mismatches quickly.

This hands-on walkthrough ties together the prior concepts into a practical test. Start by creating a new C++ Actor class named MyProjectile. Add a USphereComponent called CollisionSphere and a UProjectileMovementComponent named ProjectileMovement. In the constructor set the sphere radius, SetCollisionProfileName to your Projectile profile or a reasonable default, then call SetGenerateOverlapEvents(true) and SetNotifyRigidBodyCollision(true). Bind the OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnComponentHit delegates with AddDynamic to UFUNCTION handlers you declare in the header. Implement OnOverlapBegin to UE_LOG the OtherActor name and optionally Destroy the projectile; implement OnHit to log impact location and NormalImpulse. Compile and create a Blueprint from this class for easy placement. Next create a simple pickup actor with a UBoxComponent set to Overlap the Pawn and to Overlap the Projectile channel; in its OnComponentBeginOverlap handler call Destroy on the pickup. Place both actors and a static wall in the level. Play the level and spawn a projectile: observe an overlap log when passing through the pickup and a hit log when colliding with the wall. If events do not appear, run through the debug checklist: check object types, Generate Overlap Events, and the editor's Show Collision view. This exercise demonstrates both event types in a single playable scene and reinforces how configuration drives behavior.

These three concept cards capture the essentials you should carry forward. First: Collision Primitives — prefer simple shapes like sphere, box, and capsule for efficient and reliable detection. Second: Collision Presets and Channels — use presets for fast setup and custom channels/object types for precise filtering between game roles. Third: Overlap vs Hit — overlaps are non-blocking notifications requiring Generate Overlap Events, while hits require blocking responses and physics or notify flags to generate impact events. These rules explain both common successes and why events sometimes never fire. Keep a debug checklist handy: verify object types, responses, flags, bindings, and use the editor’s collision visualization and UE_LOG output. With these ideas you can design pickups, triggers, and physical interactions that behave predictably and scale well. Before you continue, keep these reminders in mind. Reminder one: prefer primitive shapes for collision to keep queries fast and predictable. Reminder two: collision presets are helpful but inspect the response matrix and use custom channels when you need precise filtering. Reminder three: correctly enable Generate Overlap Events, Notify Rigid Body Collision, or Simulate Physics depending on whether you expect overlap callbacks or hit notifications. When an event does not fire, use the editor collision visualization and UE_LOG to find which configuration is mismatched. These simple rules will save you time when debugging gameplay interactions and help you design interactions that scale across many actors. Which reminder will you apply first in your next prototype?
